As for the aran jumper: I've lived in Ireland for years, the reason why they are soft now is because irish wool isn't used. Irish sheep live in the climate, so their wool is coarse - nowadays that wool is used for carpets. Unprocessed wool from irish sheep was rough and oily (lanolin) so it was very protective from the elements. It was used by fishermen, but today's version is the capitalism version of it. Also as for the symbols and meaning, the fishermen's wives knitted the jumpers (obviously, although probably mothers and sisters etc for unmarried men, not really relevant for the point) and when it would get too warm, all the fishermen would take the jumpers off and put them on a pile. Because they were all the same, no-one knew which one belonged to who so the women started knitting patterns (symbols) so the men could recognise their own jumper. Over time, those symbols became family symbols, and nowadays are associated with families (clann in irish). Then the marketing stuff happened you were talking about. Just thought I'd add the info 😊

Speaking of invented myths surrounding the Aran sweater, there's a lot of similar ones surrounding the Nordic sweaters. 
First of all, the sweaters aren't really Icelandic in the first place, they're Faroese and many Faroese knitters are pretty annoyed that their national style of sweater has generically become known as "Icelandic sweaters" (and apparently also "Norwegian sweaters" in USA which is even further from the truth). The specific design with a half circle pattern around the neck, which you call an "Icelandic Lopapeysa" is a modern Norwegian invention from the 1930s, which was inspired by traditional Inuit folk costumes from Greenland, and were made during a time where Norway tried to claim Greenland and this design was part of that campaign to invent a Norwegian claim on Greenland. It was later adopted as a symbol of Icelandic nationalism despite having no Icelandic ties, being created by a Norwegian who was inspired by Greenlanders...
Real traditional patterned Faroese sweaters usually only have a simple repeating geometric pattern and often only uses the natural colours of the wool (cream, brown, and grey) and is quite similar to what you called a "Norwegian sweater" (which is actually originally Faroese). These patterned Faroese sweaters were called "skipstroyggja" literally ship sweater underlining their origin with fishermen.
There is also another style of Faroese fisherman sweater which is solid dark brown and has buttons on the left shoulder to help put it on over your head, which is called "myrkamorreyðum troyggja" meaning dark brown sweater.
Scandinavian (as opposed to Nordic) sweaters are more in the style of the Norwegian Lusekofte though similar styles existed all over Scandinavia. They often had buttons on the neck like a henley shirt and striped patterns (like a Breton shirt) were very popular along with stars and other geometric shapes. They were usually made in white and blue or white and red, and of course white, red, and blue specifically in case of the modern Norwegian sweaters because of nationalism, though the old examples typically didn't mix blue and red. These sweaters were usually worn by farmers, not sailors, and are preserved in some places as part of the folk costumes.
Lastly, I there is also a Danish variant of the dark blue gansey sweater which has a bubble pattern on the chest and upper arms that the brand SNS Herning at least claims to have invented, and has since been copied by a few others. I don't know whether these were ever actually home made or just commercially produced, but they have been around since at least since the 1920s and thus relatively old even if they aren't truly a traditional sweater. These are usually called "sømandstrøje" meaning seaman sweater.

I think you may have misunderstood what “oiled wool” is. My understanding is that for most wool, the natural oil, Lanolin, is washed out before it is spun into yarns (Lanolin is useful byproduct that’s used extensively in other products including cosmetics). With oiled wool, the Lanolin is retained. I believe it makes for an even more water-resistant fabric than ‘normal’ wool. Oiled wool sweaters appear to be popular among the UK yachting community, hence they are sold by yacht chandlers like Arthur Beale and Co.

The sweaters where it doesn’t matter which is front or back have what is known as a “boat neck”.

One thing not mentioned directly is that wool has tradeoffs between softness, durability, and warmth. That applies to the fibers themselves, the yarn, and the knit fabric. Softer wools generally pill easier and wear faster than scratchier wool. Cashmere and merino are often mixed with other fibers for strength (be sure to check the label if you're hoping for 100% cashmere or merino). Tighter yarns are less soft and less insulating but more durable. Similar with worsted spun vs woolen spun yarn. Tightly knit fabric (e.g. traditional ganseys) is less flexible and less insulating, but it's more durable and more wind resistant.

Oh, and it's worth noting that some people just have really sensitive skin, so even the really soft wools aren't skin friendly to them. This is the source of many arguments about whether a given type of wool is "scratchy" or not.

Also I believe the stitch on the Patagonia  sweater is a half fisherman’s rib or half brioche stitch. Each is worked differently but they are almost identical in their end result depending on the tension of the knitter. But that’s how you get the “knits” on one side and the “squished knits” on the other that you were describing. 

Half fisherman’s rib is a stitch where the knits on one side are essentially undone by knitting into the row below. This causes the stitches on either side to appear “squished” on the reverse side of the fabric because for each knit stitch on one side there are two on the other. 
Half brioche is basically the same thing but instead of undoing a knit by knitting below you just set it up as an undone stitch on the fist pass to begin with and then resolve it with a knit stitch on the second pass. 

These two stitches are ticker than regular rib because each row is essentially knit one and a half times. This takes up more yarn to make but results in a loftier knit fabric that doesn’t necessarily look or act like a rib even though it technically is. 
Hope that helps.

There is so much land which is super rocky & hilly with very little soil, impossible to plough or farm crops, sheep were the only way to make use of the land in these areas.
I think the association with fishing is because of its place of origin & the reputation for good fishing spots & fresh tasty fish that comes into Galway bay.

The fireproof metal trash cans in every room were replaced with melty, toxic ones.
Never hire a person with a hotel course and expect competence in a marine environment.

The reason maybe, why in German there's no (original) word for sweater/ jumper:
(The (now) used word is Pulli as short for Pullover, which is an English word, obviously.) 
The German weather is very changeable and you can't rely on one and the same outfit throughout the whole day, most of the time. Like in autumn, it can already be freezing cold in the morning, but mild/ warm in the afternoon. Kids often walk to school in gloves and thick jackets but play outside in a t-shirt after school. 
Therefore we heavily rely on layering and being able to take off pieces easily. Therefore the traditional German version of a sweater/ jumper actually is a "Strickjacke" (knit-jacket). A "sweater with buttons" comes off way easier than a sweater you have to pull over (name !) your head & hair.

Oiled sweaters mean the natural lanolin in the wool hasn't been completely bleached/washed out by harsh chemicals. It makes the wool feel nicer to the touch and also helps waterproof it. If you hand-wash the raw wool and just gently soak it, as opposed to scrubbing and using harsh chemicals (bleach is often used to make the color more uniform for mass production) obviously that's less efficient but the quality of the products it's used to make will be better, in part because the natural lanolin remains. 

As for the reason that mass produced cashmere pills so easily, it's because even with long staple fibers, the factories will chop up the fibers into tiny pieces so the sweaters all come out as identical as possible, again a mass production thing wherein the company needs to produce a whole lot of identical items for sale. Not only does it pill and shed easier, holes form a lot easier and the yarns are easy to pull apart. The longer the staple the stronger the yarn/thread it can make.

The Irish nit sweater came about in the early 1900s; ireland.  The gurnsey/jersery sweater are much older.  There are photos from the late 1800 when cameras came around.  They have a unique design, different fron the irsh cable fishermen sweaters.  The G/J sweaters are from the costal areas of England.  Theyhave gussets under the arm and sometimes before the neck shaping.  Mary Thomas documented the patterns from different villages as well as the designs and published her findings in a little fameous book.  This tsk was supported/requested by the royality of her time.  The G/J sweaters were knit in dark blue tightly wound four/five ply yarn.  The collar was almost stand up or turtle nevk and the sleeves ended on the arm to avoid getting water soaked at the wrist. Villagers tended to make up their own patterns thereby allowing some identification of village-family.  The GJ were knit in the round with side (possibly) purl stitches knitted in to denote the side seams.  Patterns in the usa were scant. sprinnerin produced books on the sweaters. Before they took off in more recent times.  The Irish Fishermen sweaters were avaible for purchase; i’m not aware that the G/J sweaters had that type of marketing.  The brish G/J and Irsh sweaters were knit from wool. The Irish sweaters used more cable patterns while the G/J had patterns from combinations of knit-purl stitches.  Evenutally information designs were shared and synthetic yarns were introduced.  I have knitted lots of G/J sweaters from the 1970s.  Love the history, process and patterns.  This is a summary of I recall, so consider my age and memory.  An american granny.  My favorite sweater pattern was the Flags of Whitby from Thomas’ book.

I suppose the quietness of the fabric makes it good for hunting, but I always think of it as layer underneath a more windproof shell.  If you're only using it for an insulating layer, you want it thick, but it doesn't have to be at all wind resistant.  It can even have big gaps in it like a knitted "afghan" throw that's on the back of my couch.

The "holes" are air pockets.  The sweater gives you loft, and the shell on the outside traps the air.  The tighter-weave sweaters for wearing on the outside are kind of a different thing, to me.    The nice thing about the more open weaves is you get the same amount of insulating power with less weight.

I still like layering up in wool, with a good sweater under a Filson mackinaw.  The mackinaw doesn't provide a whole lot of warmth (loft), but it sheds rain (Filson leaves the lanolin in the wool), and the tight weave blocks the wind.  If I get too warm, I shed the sweater that's underneath.

If I'm working outside, I don't need much under the mackinaw.  When I stop moving, a mackinaw alone doesn't do much in freezing conditions.  That's when the sweater goes back on.

The classic, black-and-white plaid mackinaw is made for winter hunting.  Silent, windproof, and it breaks up your outline in the snow.

I used to like Filson a lot more than I do, now.  They discontinued their 4-season rain jacket, which, when treated with some wax or oil, is the perfect, spacious, bulletproof, all-season wind and rain shell.  I got it, because I've had to crawl under vehicles in the mud for either repairs or recovery when stuck.  That rain jacket was what you wanted for those situations.  Of course, I never once had to roll around in the mud after I had enough money and foresight to spend $400 on a shelter-cloth shell.

Anyway, Filson used to have great info on all their gear, what made it special, precisely what materials were used and how they were processed.  Now, it's trying to be Amazon or something.

I see all the hiking enthusiasts extolling this or that space-age fabric, and I can see maybe carrying some of that stuff in your pack as spares, but if you have a good base layer, a good sweater, and a tough, waxed-cotton outer shell, you're not worried about how small it packs, because you're wearing it, every day.  If it's wool, it doesn't "stink up" for days, and you can just air it out and it's good as new.  Maybe break out that super-duper down jacket for lollygagging around camp while you air out your work gear.
